parsed_answer.content:
In the context of the JVM's Generational Garbage Collection hypothesis, the Young Generation is partitioned into three distinct regions: the Eden Space and two Survivor Spaces (S0 and S1, often referred to as From and To spaces). The Eden Space is the primary allocation site for nearly all newly instantiated objects. Because most objects exhibit high mortality rates—dying shortly after creation—Eden is designed for rapid, high-frequency allocation. When Eden fills up, a Minor GC event is triggered, utilizing a copying collector algorithm. This process identifies live objects in Eden and moves them to one of the Survivor spaces.

The Survivor Spaces act as a filter to prevent short-lived objects from prematurely migrating to the Old Generation (Tenured space). By maintaining two Survivor spaces, the JVM ensures that at any given time, one space is empty, allowing for a compacting copy operation that eliminates fragmentation. Objects that survive multiple GC cycles increment an 'age' counter in their object header. Once an object reaches a specific tenured threshold—governed by the MaxTenuringThreshold parameter—it is promoted to the Old Generation. This generational segregation drastically improves performance by allowing the JVM to focus collection efforts on the Young Generation where the majority of garbage resides, thereby minimizing the duration of Stop-The-World pauses.

items: The JVM uses a 'Copying' algorithm for the Young Generation: during a Minor GC, live objects are moved from Eden and the current 'From' Survivor space into the 'To' Survivor space, effectively compacting memory and resetting the 'From' space for the next cycle.

The Survivor spaces are managed by the 'SurvivorRatio' JVM flag, which dictates the size ratio between Eden and the Survivor spaces; improper tuning here can lead to premature promotion (tenuring) if Survivor spaces are too small to hold the live object set.
Object headers contain a 4-bit age field, allowing for a maximum tenuring threshold of 15; if an object survives 15 cycles, it is forced into the Old Generation regardless of current memory pressure.
TLABs (Thread Local Allocation Buffers) are utilized within Eden to allow threads to allocate objects without needing global locks, significantly reducing contention in multi-threaded applications.

parsed_answer.content: A common production pitfall is the 'Survivor Overflow' scenario. If your application creates many long-lived objects that don't die in Eden, they fill up the Survivor spaces. Once the Survivor space capacity is exceeded, the JVM performs 'Handle Promotion'—moving objects directly to the Old Generation. This causes premature aging and can lead to frequent Major GC events (Full GC) because the Old Generation fills up faster than expected. If you see high promotion rates in your GC logs, consider increasing the Survivor space size rather than just increasing the overall heap.
